Simple Present, Present Continuous, and Be Going to, to Explain What Data Validation Means
Present simple, present continuous and be going to are time tenses we use to express our ideas depending on specific circumstances.

PRESENT SIMPLE
Use present simple forms to refer to routines and general ideas that take place at a general time or with some sort of frequency.

To conjugate a verb in present simple you simply add an “s” or “es” to the third person singular, depending on the verb.

Examples:

 Use the following structure to make sentences in present simple.

Subject + Verb + complement.


Example:
She works for a software company.

Use the following structure to make questions in present simple.

Do/Does + subject + verb + complement + ?


Example:

Do you know any good program to validate data?
Does the IT engineer know how to validate data?

Use the following structure to make negative statements in present simple.

Subject + do/does not + verb + complement.


I don't have any idea about programming!
She doesn't come to the company on Mondays.

Note that regardless the person in interrogative and negative forms, the verb is without conjugation. We call that a “bare infinitive or infinitive without to.”

IMPORTANT:

For any other verb different from the verb to be, we use the auxiliary verb “do” to make questions and negative statements.
Compare:

Do you know how to validate data with Excel?
Are you happy?
Does he work here?
Is she here?

PRESENT CONTINUOUS

We use present continuous forms to express ongoing actions, that means actions that are taking place at the moment of speaking or actions that are temporarily happening in the present.
Use this structure to make sentences in present continuous form:
Subject+ (Aux) be + main verb+ ing+ complement

Example:

- He is calling his manager right away.
- She is working in an important project now.

In order to make questions you use the following structure:
(wh) + be + subject + ing + complement + ?


Example:
What are you doing with that computer?
Are you working on the data validation project?

BE GOING TO

You can use “be going to” to talk about plans in the future based on prior decisions or to make predictions based on present evidence.
The structure is very simple:
Subject + be going to + verb + complement.


Example:

We are going to have a meeting later.
Diane is going to be in charge of the project.

In its negative form we use the following structure:
Subject + be + not + going to + verb + complement.


Example:
Shannon is not going to finish that project for tomorrow.
I'm not going to fix the program if I don't know what the problem is.

For the interrogative form we use the following structure:
(Wh) + Be + Subject + going to + verb + complement + ?


Examples:
Why is she going to be the new leader?
Are you going to implement that code in the system?

Infinitives of Purpose Review
You can use the infinitive form of the verb (to) to show the purpose of an action.
We can use data validation processes to ensure that the kind and length of characters that people input in a text box correspond to the ones we expect.
The program by means of the data type validation process is going to verify those numbers and symbols to check if they are valid or allowed.
Use data validation processes to restrict the input of unwanted data.

You can use the infinitive of purpose to show the reason why someone does something.

The infinitive of purpose shows the reason why the subject of the sentence does what he/she does; therefore, if the subject is different from the one showing the purpose you use “so that”

Compare:

Jane is coding the program to validate all the data we have in the server.

Jane is coding the program so that the IT department validates the data we have in the server.

If you notice, in the first example, the reason why Jane is coding the program is to validate data, but in the second example, the reason why she is coding the program is for other people to validate the data.

In a more formal context you can use in order to or so as to.
Compare:
Johnna works hard to make her family happy.
The IT department works hard in order to make the data validation tools be up to date.
Both companies work together so as to safeguard their information.

images.text:
Peter: Today, we're going to start this session by discussing what data validation is for. So, any volunteers?
Mark: Well, If not mistaken, we can use data validation processes to ensure that the kind and length of characters that people input in a text box correspond to the ones we expect.

Peter: Excellent. For example, right now, I'm trying to type numbers, letters, and symbols into this text entry box that only accepts numbers. The program by means of the data type validation process is going to verify those numbers and symbols to check if they are valid or allowed; notice the program is not letting me do so, because of the restriction. This process, as you can see, involves two different steps: the validation check that verifies if the data is valid or not and the post check action, where the post validation process sends feedback to correct possible errors.

Mark: Excuse me, but does that mean that we can use data validation processes to restrict the input of unwanted data?
Peter: Of course, if you set the proper restrictions, the data validation process gives you accuracy and consistency of data input to apps and systems.
Mark: Ok. That's interesting. Would you mind giving me some more examples?

Peter: In computer science, data validation may warrant a program works correctly in accordance with the data you provide. But, you must be sure about the restrictions you set when you are coding the program; you must also know that these restrictions are the same validation rules. If you know how to work with them, such rules are going to provide you with security in all the data that you input to the system.
Mark: Thanks for the explanation.
Peter: Next session we are going to learn how to work with data validation processes in programs, such as Excel.
